latin.527: Nam, si dixeris eum corruptionem haereditariam praetermisisse, sequentur duo: Unum, eam ex hac tota collatione, quam inter primum & secundum Adamum Apostolus instituit, colligi non posse. Non enim alia mala ex Adamo in genus humanum manasse sequentibus versibus docet, quam quae hoc v. 12. nominavit. Id autem Pighii causam valde iuvabit.
latin.528: & quamvis alia extent in sacris literis loca, ex quibus effici possit, nos nasci corruptos peccato, tamen fere alius nullus est, qui eam corruptionem doceat ab ipso Adamo profectam in omnes homines invasisse.
latin.529: Alterum, aut eam corruptionem nullam esse, aut Apostolum aberrasse a suo scopo. Si prius, vicerunt Pelagiani, estque adhuc in integro liberum arbitrium. Posterius patet.
latin.530: Scopus enim Apostoli est docere quae mala a primo Adamo, quae contra bona a secundo Adamo in genus humanum fluxerint, ut intelligamus mirum non esse, cum unus homo ad nos perdendos tam potens fuerit, unum hominem, Iesum Christum, nos posse servare. Itaque bona ab hoc in nos profecta malis ab illo profectis accurate comparat. Quis igitur credat eum voluisse id malum silentio praeterire, quod constat & ex Adamo in nos derivari, & causam omnium nostrorum peccatorum esse?
latin.531: Si vero dixeris, Apostolum mortis nomine corruptionem illam haereditariam, quae peccatum est, comprehendisse, primum discedes ab omnium (quos viderim) interpretum consensu. Deinde causam Pelagianorum adversus Augustinum iuvabis, mortis nomen de morte animae accipientium.
latin.532: Tum Apostolum induces contra suum morem nomine mortis absolute posito, & sine ulla additione, eiusmodi corruptionem significantem, unumque & idem nomen semel positum, semel intelligendum, simul proprie & figurate accipientem. Praeterea, quis credat mortem cum a peccato distinguitur, ut fit hoc loco, peccatum significare?

pass_a.527: Say he skipped hereditary corruption, and two consequences land. One: you cannot pull it from Paul's whole first-Adam / second-Adam collation. Later verses name no other Adam-evils into the race than v. 12 already listed—music to Pighius's ears.
pass_a.528: Other sacred places may show we are born corrupt with sin; almost none teaches that this corruption, streaming from Adam himself, overran every human. That scarcity matters here.
pass_a.529: The other fork: either corruption is nothing, or Paul missed his mark. Take the first and Pelagius wins—free will still whole. The second needs no proof.
pass_a.530: For Paul's aim is to teach what evils flowed from the first Adam, and what goods by contrast from the second, into the human race—so we see it is no wonder that, when one man was so powerful to ruin us, one man, Jesus Christ, can save us. So he carefully compares goods from this one with evils from that. Who then believes he meant to pass in silence that evil which both derives from Adam into us and is the cause of all our sins?
pass_a.531: But if you say he packed that hereditary corruption—which is sin—under the name of death: first you leave the consent of all interpreters I have seen. Next you help the Pelagians against Augustine, who take 'death' as death of the soul.
pass_a.532: Then you make Paul, against his custom, with 'death' set absolutely and with no addition, mean such corruption—and one and the same name, set once, to be taken once, yet both properly and figuratively at once. Besides, who believes death, when distinguished from sin as here, signifies sin? Tip before the all-are-sinners proof.

527: For if you shall say that he passed over hereditary corruption, two things will follow: One, that it cannot be gathered from this whole collation which the Apostle instituted between the first and the second Adam. For in the following verses he does not teach that other evils flowed from Adam into the human race than those which he named in this v. 12. But that will greatly help Pighius's cause.
528: And although there are other places in the sacred letters from which it can be made out that we are born corrupt with sin, yet there is almost no other which teaches that that corruption, proceeding from Adam himself, invaded into all humans. That scarcity matters here.
529: The other, either that that corruption is nothing, or that the Apostle wandered from his aim. If the former, the Pelagians have won, and free choice is still intact. The latter is plain.
530: For the Apostle's aim is to teach what evils from the first Adam, what goods by contrast from the second Adam, flowed into the human race, so that we may understand it is not wonderful, when one man was so powerful to destroy us, that one man, Jesus Christ, can save us. And so he accurately compares the goods proceeded from this one into us with the evils proceeded from that one. Who therefore would believe that he wished to pass over in silence that evil which it is agreed both is derived from Adam into us, and is the cause of all our sins?
531: But if you shall say that the Apostle comprehended that hereditary corruption, which is sin, under the name of death, first you will depart from the consent of all interpreters (whom I have seen). Next you will help the cause of the Pelagians against Augustine, who take the name of death of the death of the soul.
532: Then you will bring in the Apostle against his custom, with the name of death set absolutely, and without any addition, signifying corruption of that kind, and one and the same name set once, to be understood once, taking it at once properly and figuratively. Besides, who would believe that death, when it is distinguished from sin, as is done in this place, signifies sin?
